t: The Young Turks were a diverse network of exiles, students, officers and intellectuals, many of them Albanians, Arabs, Armenians, Kurds or Jews, united by opposition to Abdul Hamid II and the wish to restore the constitution of 1876.
Their Committee of Union and Progress forced the sultan to restore the constitution on 24 July 1908, opening the Second Constitutional Era and the country’s first multi-party democracy.
After the 1913 Raid on the Sublime Porte the CUP ruled as a dictatorship, took the empire into the First World War and masterminded the genocides of Ottoman Christians from 1915 to 1917.
dyk: The Committee of Union and Progress owes its name to Auguste Comte’s positivist motto “Order and Progress”: in 1894 Ahmed Rıza asked the society to call itself Order and Progress, and its members compromised on Union and Progress.
ev: Medical students including Ibrahim Temo and Abdullah Cevdet form a secret society, the beginning of the Committee of Union and Progress
The First Congress of Ottoman Opposition, in Paris, splits over whether to invite foreign intervention
The Second Congress of Ottoman Opposition agrees that Abdul Hamid II must be deposed, without foreign interference
Unionist officers of the Third Army mutiny and the sultan restores the constitution, opening the Second Constitutional Era
After the Raid on the Sublime Porte a radicalized CUP takes power and bans all other parties
The CUP takes the Ottoman Empire into the First World War on the side of the Central Powers
The genocides of Armenians, Assyrians and other Ottoman Christians, masterminded within the CUP
The CUP ministry resigns, the Armistice of Mudros is signed, and Enver, Talaat and Cemal flee into exile

f.where: The Ottoman Empire, above all Constantinople and Macedonia, where Thessalonica and the Third Army were its base; exile circles in Paris, London, Geneva, Bucharest, Cairo and Brussels.
f.period: Secret societies of students and cadets after 1889; exile, schisms and repression in the 1890s; the opposition congresses of 1902 and 1907 and the Ottoman Freedom Society (1906); the Young Turk Revolution (1908); the Second Constitutional Era and party rivalry (1908–1913); one-party rule of the CUP and the First World War (1913–1918).
f.figures: Ibrahim Temo and Abdullah Cevdet, medical students who founded the first society; Ahmed Rıza, the positivist leader in Paris; Prince Sabahaddin, champion of decentralization; Mehmed Talaat, founder of the Ottoman Freedom Society; Ahmed Niyazi Bey and Enver Pasha, leaders of the 1908 revolution; Ziya Gökalp, Turkish nationalist sociologist.
f.outcome: The constitution restored and the Second Constitutional Era opened in 1908, with multi-party politics for the first time; then a one-party state from 1913, entry into the First World War on the side of the Central Powers, and the genocides of Ottoman Christians of 1915 to 1917, masterminded within the CUP; its leaders fled into exile in 1918.
